opening_message:
Ticket 1: Kenneth Burch (employee ID E007) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E007.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Kenneth Burch (E007) is a full-time Analyst. Requested write access to Payroll. As a full-time employee, the maximum is write (admin would require the Payroll Specialist role, which the Analyst role does not own). Requested level is at the maximum, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security record shows Kenneth Burch (E007) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Since training is basic, maximum is read. Requested write exceeds maximum, so recommend read.
reason: The HR and Security notes conflict on Kenneth Burch's (E007) employment type. HR states full-time Analyst (max write for Payroll, so write would be allowed), while Security states contractor with basic training (max read for Payroll). Given this unresolved discrepancy, I apply the more restrictive, safe interpretation: granting read is valid under both scenarios (full-time may have read or write; contractor with basic training may only have read), and I cannot grant write without risking a policy violation. Granting read also never exceeds the requested write level.
